slides.title: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA
paragraphs: This project asks a specific question: once a kidney transplant biopsy has been collected, can its RNA measurements classify the rejection diagnosis recorded for that tissue? I will explain the measurements, compare four models, and show the prediction software.
actions: State the research question, then introduce transplant rejection.
visible_cues: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA

slides.title: Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A kidney biopsy is a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination. It can supply two kinds of evidence. A specialist examines thin sections under a microscope for injury and inflammation. Histology means studying tissue this way. Molecular measurements count selected types of RNA, which include messages cells make when genes are active. Those counts provide the inputs to this model.

In this dataset, the recorded diagnoses come from histological assessment. The authors rescored transplant biopsies using Banff 2019 criteria. Those diagnoses provide the answers used to train and evaluate the classifier. The molecular measurements provide its inputs.
Why seek another assessment when the tissue has already been examined? That is the reason for the proposed use on the next slide.
actions: Explain the two forms of evidence beneath the biopsy definition and distinguish the recorded diagnosis from the model inputs.
visible_cues: Rejection: the recipient's immune system attacks the donated kidney.
Kidney biopsy: a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination.
Histology: microscopic examination reveals injury and inflammation and supports the recorded diagnosis.
Molecular measurements: counts of selected RNA types provide the model's inputs.

slides.title: Possible Use: Molecular Second Opinion for Ambiguous Biopsies
paragraphs: The possible use is a molecular second opinion for ambiguous biopsies. Sometimes the microscopic findings are borderline or conflict with other clinical evidence. A specialist then needs to weigh the available information.

The first box gives a hypothetical example. A biopsy shows mild inflammation, but the microscopic findings do not clearly establish rejection. That leaves the specialist with an uncertain interpretation of tissue already collected.

Histology shows tissue appearance. RNA messages provide information about gene activity in that tissue. Because they describe different things, a molecular assessment could add useful evidence for specialist review.

This project tests how well RNA measurements classify recorded rejection diagnoses and builds software that can score further specimens. In the second hypothetical box, the RNA pattern receives a high rejection score. In a validated application, that could give the specialist additional evidence when reviewing the uncertain biopsy.

The example explains the proposed use. My current evaluation does not establish that the score resolves this uncertainty. The next study would compare assessment with and without the molecular score in difficult cases.
actions: Read the first hypothetical example, explain the project question, then continue the example in the matching box.

slides.title: Evidence for a molecular second opinion
paragraphs: There is a clinical research basis for this proposal. Banff guidance supports the classification of transplant biopsy findings and considers validated molecular tests in selected difficult cases.

Rosales and colleagues used B-HOT, the same fixed panel of RNA measurements used here. Patients who later developed chronic active antibody-mediated rejection had higher initial rejection-related molecular scores as a group, despite lacking that diagnosis on the initial biopsy. Antibody-mediated rejection is a form involving immune proteins called antibodies.

That study supports investigating information beyond the initial tissue diagnosis. Its later-outcome finding belongs to that external study. This project measures agreement with recorded diagnoses. Its value in ambiguous biopsies needs direct evaluation.
actions: Explain the two evidence rows, then connect them to the project question.

slides.title: What the dataset contains
paragraphs: The public data come in two downloads: a metadata file and an archive containing 1,395 individual count files. My code assembles them into the two tables shown here.

The count table has one row per biopsy specimen and a column for each of the 770 RNA counts. The specimen-information table contains the recorded diagnosis and the study group assigned by the authors.
Specimen ID is unique in each table and matches the rows one to one. GSM6510425 is the same specimen in both. This pairs the measurements with the diagnosis used for training and evaluation.

The 1,395 specimens include 1,193 transplant biopsies and 202 native-kidney controls. All enter my comparison. The article reports those control counts, but the public specimen metadata do not identify which no-rejection rows are native kidneys.

slides.title: Outcome: rejection versus no rejection
paragraphs: The study records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.

Those three diagnoses all count as rejection. The fourth category, no rejection, includes normal tissue and other kidney diseases. Some diagnostic categories were excluded from the study rather than assigned to no rejection. I predict these recorded labels.
I also retain the original diagnoses. That will let me see whether the missed cases are concentrated in a particular kind of rejection.

slides.title: The measurements used to build the features
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 RNA counts, one for each RNA type measured. Each count summarizes signals from that type of RNA. There are two roles for those measurements.
The 758 on the left include human and viral RNA measurements. The counts describe the tissue as a whole. A higher signal can reflect more activity within cells, a different mixture of cells, or both.

The other 12 measure housekeeping RNAs selected to provide a relatively stable reference. I use them to adjust for differences in how much measurable RNA each specimen supplies. The next slide shows that adjustment.
actions: Use the 758 and 12 groups to explain the role of each set of counts.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: For each of the 758 counts, I use the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in my public example, starting with its raw count of four.
Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.
Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.
actions: Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.
visible_cues: For each of the 758 RNA counts / IFNG example
1. Start with the raw count: 4
2. Calculate log2(count + 1): 2.322
3. Average log2(count + 1) for the 12 reference RNAs: 7.900
4. Subtract that reference: 2.322 − 7.900 = −5.578

slides.title: Development and evaluation specimens
paragraphs: The authors supplied two groups, or cohorts. Discovery has 1,050 specimens and validation has 345. This project preserves that division for model development and the final comparison.

Within discovery, a saved split assigns 787 specimens to training and 263 to screening, keeping the four diagnosis proportions similar. Training fits the models. Screening compares candidates and chooses the threshold for a rejection flag.
I then evaluate the selected model and threshold on the same 345 validation specimens used by every comparison model. The authors call this technical validation.

The full study does not document patient or referring-center separation across the groups. It reports referrals from several regions, but all specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories. Geographic breadth does not establish separation by patient or referring center.

slides.title: Models compared
paragraphs: Each model produces a score for rejection versus no rejection. The models estimate probabilities, but calibration has not established reliable individual probabilities here. I therefore call the output a model score.
The constant model uses the training rejection fraction for everyone. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.

IFNG encodes interferon gamma, an immune-signalling protein. The study associates it with T-cell-mediated rejection. It is an understandable one-measurement benchmark, fixed in my starting recipe. I did not establish it as the best individual predictor.

Logistic regression combines the 758 measurements using learned weights. Regularization limits those weights to reduce overfitting. CatBoost combines decision trees, allowing more complicated relationships between measurements and diagnoses.

The models use the same specimens. The RNA models start with the same normalization. I can ask whether combining measurements helps and whether CatBoost improves enough over logistic regression to justify its complexity.
actions: Explain each model in table order.

IFNG only: one immune-related RNA measurement as a simple benchmark

CatBoost: a combination of decision trees

slides.title: Choosing a rejection threshold
paragraphs: A threshold turns a model score into a rejection flag. Recall is the proportion of recorded rejection cases detected. False negatives are missed cases. Precision is the proportion of positive flags with recorded rejection. False positives are incorrect flags.

On screening specimens, first retain thresholds with at least 90 percent recall. Among those choices, minimize false positives. Keep the chosen model and threshold together for evaluation. Minimizing false positives here maximizes specificity. It does not mean maximizing precision.
This gives priority to detecting rejection, then reduces incorrect flags. The 90 percent target is an experiment choice. It is not an established clinical requirement or a guarantee on new data.

The clinical tradeoff depends on what follows the score. The source study highlights infection controls because mistaking infection for rejection could lead to harmful additional immunosuppression. False positives therefore matter as well as misses. My project has not measured those downstream consequences.
Threshold selection also does not calibrate scores. The saved threshold appears in the demonstration.
actions: Define recall and precision through their associated errors, then explain the screening rule and why its 90 percent target is an experiment choice.
visible_cues: Recall: proportion of recorded rejection cases detected (false negatives are missed cases).
Precision: proportion of positive flags with recorded rejection (false positives are incorrect flags).
Selection using screening specimens
1. Detect at least 90% of recorded rejection cases.*
2. Among qualifying choices, minimize false positives.
3. Keep the chosen model and threshold for evaluation.
*The 90% target is an experiment choice, not an established clinical requirement.

slides.title: Validation results
paragraphs: Here are the results on the same 345 validation specimens. False negatives are missed cases among the 169 specimens recorded as rejection. False positives are incorrect flags among the 176 recorded as no rejection. The count labels let me compare both errors directly.

The constant model flags every specimen at its selected threshold. It has zero false negatives out of 169 rejection specimens, but 176 false positives out of 176 no-rejection specimens. That shows why finding every rejection case alone does not make a useful classifier.
The IFNG-only model has 14 false negatives and 75 false positives. It detects many rejection cases, but also produces many incorrect positive flags.
Logistic regression uses all 758 normalized measurements. It has 33 false negatives and eight false positives. CatBoost has 25 false negatives and also eight false positives.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false positives but 11 more false negatives. Its validation recall is 85.2 percent, below the 90 percent screening target. The criterion used during development gives a different result in this evaluation group.

If the intended use prioritizes avoiding missed rejection, those additional false negatives matter. I cannot settle the preferred tradeoff from total error counts alone. I would need to know how specialists act on the score and what those actions change.

Compared with logistic regression, CatBoost detects eight more rejection specimens with the same false-positive count. Combining measurements reduces false positives here. The smaller difference between the two models using all measurements needs closer examination before I treat it as a dependable advantage.
actions: State both denominators before comparing the bars. Pause on the IFNG tradeoff, the recall shortfall, and the eight-case difference from logistic regression.

slides.title: Most CatBoost misses were T-cell rejection
paragraphs: The original diagnoses help me examine CatBoost's 25 misses. It missed six of 56 antibody-mediated specimens, 18 of 95 T-cell-mediated specimens, and one of 18 mixed specimens.

T-cell rejection accounts for most misses and is also the largest rejection group. About 19 percent of that group was missed, compared with about 11 percent of the antibody-mediated group. One miss among only 18 mixed specimens gives limited evidence about what to expect elsewhere.

Overall, the model detects 144 of 169 rejection specimens, or 85.2 percent. This is recall, also called sensitivity. On screening, it detected 157 of 174, or 90.2 percent. The validation result is below the 90 percent requirement I used to choose the threshold.

So the screening rule cannot guarantee performance on new specimens. These errors describe disagreements with the recorded diagnoses. Resolving individual disagreements would require review of the tissue and clinical records.

slides.title: The advantage over logistic regression is uncertain
paragraphs: CatBoost detects eight more of the 169 rejection specimens than logistic regression. Each makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. How dependable is that difference?

The first comparison holds the fitted models fixed. I repeatedly resample the validation specimens, allowing a specimen to appear more than once. Both models use the same draws. The 95 percent interval for their difference in detection includes zero, so these results do not establish a clear advantage for CatBoost.

The second comparison asks how the development choice changes with a different split. This follow-up repeats development with 20 saved discovery splits. Each separates fitting, screening, and assessment. The selection rule chooses CatBoost in 13 repetitions and logistic regression in seven.

Those repetitions overlap, so they describe variation with the split. The demonstration retains the selected CatBoost model. Logistic regression remains a credible simpler option to compare in a new cohort.
actions: Explain the fixed-model comparison before the separate development-repeat results.

slides.title: Training and prediction use the same preparation
paragraphs: Training and prediction use the same preparation code. The service reads a CSV, checks the required counts, and normalizes them into 758 model inputs. It then scores those inputs with the saved model.
The command line and the web application both use this code. This matters because a difference in preparation between analysis and the application could change the results.
The response contains specimen ID, model score, threshold, rejection flag, and model version. The version identifies the saved model. The flag records whether the score crossed its threshold.

The service loads the model controlled by this project. The caller supplies the count file. Missing measurements, duplicate names, negative counts, and non-finite values produce an error and stop scoring. The next slide shows both a valid request and a missing-measurement error.

slides.title: Testing the proposed use in ambiguous biopsies
paragraphs: My current evidence is agreement with recorded diagnoses in one deposited study. The next evaluation needs to test the proposed use in ambiguous transplant biopsies.

First, evaluate new transplant biopsies with patient and center identifiers and documented laboratory quality checks. This would address the current inclusion of native-kidney controls and the unknown separation between patients and centers. Choose models and thresholds before examining those results, keeping logistic regression in the comparison.

The original study excluded some diagnostic categories, including borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection. A study of ambiguous cases should include the difficult interpretations the proposed tool is meant to support.

Compare usual assessment with assessment that includes the molecular score. Independent expert review and follow-up outcomes could help judge whether the extra evidence improves interpretation. The classifier and scoring software provide a starting point for that evaluation.

backups.title: Backup: measuring biopsy RNA with NanoString nCounter
paragraphs: RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active. Measuring those messages gives me information about activity in the biopsy tissue.

An assay is a laboratory test. NanoString nCounter is the measurement system used in this study. B-HOT is the panel: the fixed list of RNA types selected for measurement. An assay target means the type of RNA that a probe recognizes.

The laboratory extracts RNA from preserved tissue. Probes recognize selected RNAs, and NanoString nCounter counts their identifying barcodes. Each resulting count is a number associated with a named RNA measurement.
For example, IFNG is one of the measurements. Its raw count is four in the public specimen used in the preparation example and application demonstration.

paragraphs: This table compares the four models on the same 345 validation specimens. Miss counts use the 169 recorded rejection specimens. False-flag counts use the 176 recorded no-rejection specimens. Sensitivity is the fraction of rejection specimens flagged. Specificity is the fraction of no-rejection specimens left unflagged.

backups.title: Backup: normalization and model settings
paragraphs: For each RNA measurement, add one to the raw count and take its base-two logarithm. Subtract the average of the 12 housekeeping counts after applying the same log transformation. This expresses the measurement relative to the specimen's housekeeping reference. The 758 resulting values are the model inputs.

Logistic regression has one additional preparation step. For each normalized measurement, calculate its average and standard deviation across training specimens. Subtract that average and divide by that standard deviation. Reuse those same training values for screening, validation, and future requests. This puts the measurements on comparable scales. CatBoost does not use that additional scaling step here.
Logistic regression uses regularization setting C equal to 0.1. The selected CatBoost model uses 300 trees with depth four and learning rate 0.04. These settings describe the saved comparison.

backups.title: Backup: study, assay and deployment limits
paragraphs: The full article and supplements do not document the number of unique patients, a rule for repeat biopsies, or allocation that separates patients and referring centers between groups. All specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories. Specimen-level uncertainty intervals could be too narrow if some observations are related.

The evaluated dataset includes 202 native-kidney controls: 191 in discovery and 11 in validation. The public specimen metadata do not map those controls to individual records, so my current validation counts cannot be presented as a transplant-only evaluation.

The study excluded borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection, chronic inactive antibody-mediated rejection, and chronic active T-cell-mediated rejection with mild or minimal inflammation, defined as an i score below two. These specific exclusions limit evidence for those difficult categories. They do not establish that every ambiguous biopsy was excluded.

The software checks required measurements and usable numeric counts. The project did not independently repeat laboratory quality checks such as control-probe or imaging checks. Meaningful inputs still require a compatible assay and completed laboratory quality checks.

The score analysis does not establish reliable individual probabilities. The service labels its output a model score. The local research container has been tested, while cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Answer the relevant limitation and explain what additional evidence would address it.

backups.title: Backup: sources and contributions
paragraphs: Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study and the GSE212160 deposit. This project uses their raw measurements for its own rejection-versus-no-rejection comparison. It does not reconstruct their published classifier.

The project provides saved model runs, shared preparation and prediction software, and a tested local demonstration. Configurations, input hashes, reports, and source code make the quantitative claims inspectable.

The presentation guide draws on Bourne for audience and rehearsal, Kosslyn and colleagues for presentation flaws, Garner and Alley for connecting statements to evidence, and Rougier and colleagues for clear figures. AI assisted with preparing this presentation.

backups.title: Backup: UNOS research connection
paragraphs: UNOS researchers have studied whether artificial intelligence can identify anatomical issues from donor-kidney photographs. They used historical transplant and refusal records to label the images. Their stated aim includes supporting clinical decisions and making anatomical assessment more consistent.

The connection is the research approach: learn from existing assessments to develop an additional source of evidence for transplant professionals. Here, the inputs are RNA measurements and the question concerns rejection in biopsy tissue.
These are different clinical tasks. The UNOS example provides context for the approach. It does not endorse this project or establish that my classifier improves clinical decisions.
actions: Explain the different inputs and clinical questions before drawing the research connection.
